title: Cartesian fibration of categorical algebras over object spaces
statement:
Use the universe, infinity-category, space and algebroid conventions of [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. Let $\mathcal V$ be any monoidal infinity-category and let $\mathcal S$ be the infinity-category of small spaces. The projection
$$p:\operatorname{Algd}(\mathcal V)\longrightarrow\mathcal S,\qquad A\longmapsto X_A$$
is a Cartesian fibration. Here a Cartesian fibration is an inner fibration (a simplicial map having the right lifting property against every inner horn inclusion) with a Cartesian lift of every base arrow with specified target; an arrow $e:E'\to E$ over $f:X'\to X$ is Cartesian when, for every $D$, the induced square of mapping spaces with corners $\operatorname{Map}(D,E')$, $\operatorname{Map}(D,E)$, $\operatorname{Map}(pD,X')$ and $\operatorname{Map}(pD,X)$ is a homotopy pullback. The fibre at $X$ is $\operatorname{Alg}_{\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}}(\mathcal V)$. Transport along $f:X\to Y$ is restriction $f^*B$, with $(f^*B)(x,x')=B(fx,fx')$ and the restricted compositions and units. An arrow in $\operatorname{Algd}(\mathcal V)$ is $p$-Cartesian if and only if it is fully faithful. In particular, for $A$ over $X$, $B$ over $Y$ and $f:X\to Y$, the homotopy fibre over $f$ of $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Algd}(\mathcal V)}(A,B)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal S}(X,Y)$ is naturally equivalent to $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_{\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}}(\mathcal V)}(A,f^*B)$. The evaluation $\iota_0 A=\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Algd}(\mathcal V)}(E^0,A)\to X_A$ is an equivalence. For $\iota_n A=\operatorname{Map}(E^n,A)$ and $\iota A=\operatorname{colim}_{\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}}\iota_n A$ as in [def-coef-complete-algebroid], a functor $F:A\to B$ induces a surjection $\pi_0\iota A\to\pi_0\iota B$ if and only if every object of $B$ is equivalent to some $F(a)$. Here an object equivalence is a functor $E^1\to B$ with the prescribed endpoints; equivalently, it is a morphism $\mathbf1\to B(b,b')$ with a two-sided inverse up to the unit and composition homotopies. These are exactly the equivalences in the underlying category with mapping spaces $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,B(b,b'))$. Paths in $X_A$ induce equivalences between the corresponding objects in the underlying enriched category. Postcomposition by a monoidal functor $\mathcal V\to\mathcal W$ defines a functor of these Cartesian fibrations over $\mathcal S$, commuting coherently with restriction; it sends fully faithful essentially surjective arrows to such arrows.

source.place: Definitions 3.6.1 and 4.3.1 and Remark 4.3.2 (the equivalent generalized-operad model); Definition 3.6.12 and Lemma 4.3.9 (change of enrichment); Lemmas 5.1.2, 5.3.2 and 5.3.4, Proposition 5.1.15, and Definitions 5.1.8, 5.3.1, 5.3.3; mapping-space universal property of Cartesian lifts. Paths act by transport of units and reverse paths give inverse object equivalences. Read online; archive WANTED. No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical result.

proof.text:
For a map $f:X\to Y$, apply $f$ to every coordinate in the relative-nerve data for $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$. This gives $\Delta_f^{\mathrm{op}}$ over $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, with fiber map $f^{n+1}$ in degree $n$, commuting with all coordinate-selection maps. The relative-nerve theorem says that these projections are left fibrations and all their edges are cocartesian. Consequently $\Delta_f^{\mathrm{op}}$ preserves inert edges, so precomposition preserves inert-preserving algebra functors. Reindexing the same data in families of maps supplies all higher homotopies, and $(g f)^*=f^*g^*$ and $1^*=1$ with these coherences. Thus $X\mapsto\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)$ is a coherent contravariant functor on spaces.

We also verify the generalized-operad hypothesis needed in step 4. Its Segal comparisons are the adjacent-pair identifications $X^{n+1}\simeq X^2\times_X\cdots\times_X X^2$, with degree-zero fiber $X$. For tuples $x\in X^{m+1}$, $y\in X^{n+1}$ and $\phi:[m]\to[n]$ in $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, put $h=\phi^{\mathrm{op}}:[n]\to[m]$. The $K=\Delta^0$ cocartesian transport formula in the left fibration identifies the mapping-space fiber over $\phi$ with
$$\operatorname{Map}_{X^{n+1}}\bigl((x_{h(0)},\ldots,x_{h(n)}),y\bigr)\simeq\prod_{i=0}^{n}\operatorname{Path}_X(x_{h(i)},y_i).$$
Restricting to adjacent pairs gives the same product by gluing the pair path spaces over their shared vertex path spaces. This is precisely the generalized Segal mapping-space condition over the degree-zero fiber; for $n=0$ it is the single vertex path space. Together with the inner-fibration and inert-lift properties of the left fibration, this verifies that $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a generalized nonsymmetric infinity operad. It is small after the same permitted universe enlargement.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.13, 4.1.1, 4.3.1 and Remark 4.3.2; explicit relative-nerve restriction and generalized Segal mapping-space calculation using cocartesian transport

proof.text:
Choose an ambient universe in which the category $\mathcal S_{\mathcal U}$ of the original small spaces and all the fibers $\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)$ are small, and a further universe in which their category of fibrations is formed. This is possible because $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal V^\otimes$ fit in the ambient universe, every $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ is original-small, and its functor category into the ambient-small $\mathcal V^\otimes$ is ambient-small. Thus we use straightening with ambient-small base and fibers; we do not assert that $\mathcal S_{\mathcal U}$ is $\mathcal U$-small. Apply the Cartesian dual of straightening to the functor of step 1: equivalently, unstraighten $X\mapsto\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)^{\mathrm{op}}$ over $\mathcal S^{\mathrm{op}}$, then take the opposite total category. This supplies an inner-fibration representative of the total category specified in [def-coef-complete-algebroid], with fiber $\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)$, and a Cartesian arrow $c_f:f^*B\to B$ represented by the identity of $f^*B$. Transport is therefore the stated restriction, including its units and compositions. The dual of the mapping-space fiber formula for cocartesian transport, with $K=\Delta^0$, gives naturally
$$\operatorname{hofib}_f\bigl(\operatorname{Map}(A,B)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal S}(X,Y)\bigr)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)}(A,f^*B).$$
In particular the mapping-space square in the item is a homotopy pullback for $c_f$. The intrinsic formulation and the inner-fibration representative agree by straightening.

source.place: Definitions 3.6.1 and 4.3.1, Remark 4.3.2; HTT Cartesian straightening and Proposition 2.4.4.2, dual transport formula

proof.text:
Enlarge universes so that $\mathcal V$ is small in the intermediate universe and apply monoidal Yoneda. Put $\widehat{\mathcal V}=\mathcal P(\mathcal V)$ and write $J$ for postcomposition with $j^\otimes$. The cited diagram assertion, restricted to inert-preserving functors on $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$, makes every fiber functor $J_X$ fully faithful. This restriction has the required size because $X$ was small in the original universe. The unit equivalence identifies $J(E^n_{\mathcal V})$ with $E^n_{\widehat{\mathcal V}}$, compatibly with all finite-set maps. Moreover $J$ is fully faithful on total algebroid mapping spaces: step 2 identifies its fiber over every $f:X\to Y$ with the equivalence induced by $J_X$, since $J_X(f^*B)=f^*J_Y(B)$. In the larger object-space universe restrict the base to the full subcategory on the original-small spaces. Inclusion of these spaces in the larger universe does not change their mapping spaces: maps and homotopies between the original Kan complexes are the same simplicial maps. Thus both total mapping spaces lie over the same $\operatorname{Map}(X,Y)$, and the homotopy-fiber detection theorem applies. Hence
$$\operatorname{Map}(E^n_{\mathcal V},A)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(E^n_{\widehat{\mathcal V}},J A)$$
is natural in $n$ and $A$. No presentability or colimit hypothesis has been added to $\mathcal V$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 5.1.15 and proof of Theorem 5.6.6 (monoidal-presheaf universe enlargement)

proof.text: A morphism $\alpha:A\to A'$ in a fixed fiber is an equivalence exactly when every $\alpha_{x,x'}$ is an equivalence. Indeed postcompose with $j$: it preserves these equivalences, and colorwise detection in the presentably monoidal $\widehat{\mathcal V}$ says that $J_X(\alpha)$ is an equivalence of algebras. Full faithfulness of $J_X$ from step 3 reflects invertibility: lift an inverse through its equivalences on mapping spaces, and the two inverse homotopies lift as well. The converse follows by evaluating an inverse of $\alpha$ at each pair. The colors here are precisely the pairs $(x,x')$ in $X^2$, by the relative-nerve definition.

source.place: Lemma A.5.5; only its conservativity clause is used after monoidal Yoneda enlargement

proof.text:
Represent $F:A\to B$ over $f$ by $\alpha:A\to f^*B$ and factor it as $A\xrightarrow{\alpha}f^*B\xrightarrow{c_f}B$. If $\alpha$ is an equivalence, the Cartesian mapping-space square for $c_f$ remains a pullback after composing with it, so $F$ is Cartesian. Conversely if $F$ is Cartesian, compare its square with that of $c_f$, and take the fiber over the identity of $X$ for each testing algebra $D$ over $X$. Step 2 then identifies the comparison with
$$\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_X}(D,A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_X}(D,f^*B).$$
It is an equivalence for every $D$. Full faithfulness of infinity Yoneda implies that $\alpha$ is an equivalence. Step 4 identifies this condition with equivalence of every $A(x,x')\to B(fx,fx')$, which is exactly full faithfulness. This proves both directions of the Cartesian-arrow criterion rather than treating it as part of the definition of the total category.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 5.3.2, with the vertical-factor equivalence detected by infinity Yoneda

proof.text: Apply the existing equivalence-nerve theorem to $JA$ in the presentably monoidal $\widehat{\mathcal V}$. Step 3 identifies its entire simplicial equivalence nerve with $\iota_\bullet A$, over the unchanged object space. In degree zero its evaluation is therefore $\iota_0A\simeq X_A$. The same comparison shows that $\iota_\bullet A$ is a groupoid object and that the homotopy fiber of $\iota_1A\to X_A^2$ at $(a,a')$ identifies with the invertible components of $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,A(a,a'))$: full faithfulness and strong monoidality of $j$ identify this mapping space with $\operatorname{Map}_{\widehat{\mathcal V}}(\mathbf1,jA(a,a'))$, with its units and composition. Invertible means that some reverse morphism has both composites homotopic to the relevant units. Thus a map $E^1\to A$ is exactly an equivalence in the underlying category with the mapping spaces specified in the item. These comparisons commute with the two endpoint evaluations and all simplicial operators.

source.place: Lemma 5.1.2, Proposition 5.1.17 and Corollary 5.2.7 after the universe enlargement used in Proposition 5.1.15

proof.text: A path $\gamma:a\to a'$ in $X_A$ gives an equivalence of objects as follows. Take the identity element at $a$ in $\iota_1A$, whose endpoints are $(a,a)$. Together with the path $(1_a,\gamma)$ from $(a,a)$ to $(a,a')$, it is a point of the homotopy fiber of $\iota_1A\to X_A^2$ at $(a,a')$. The endpoint-compatible identification of step 6 turns this point into an object equivalence from $a$ to $a'$. Equivalently the associated map $\mathbf1\to A(a,a')$ transports the unit of $A(a,a)$ in the second coordinate. Under composition in the groupoid object of step 6, a path in the endpoint space restricts the composition homotopy at the identity to that path. Consequently the composites for $\gamma$ and its reverse are represented by $\gamma\gamma^{-1}$ and $\gamma^{-1}\gamma$; their contractions to constant paths give the two unit homotopies. Restricting this composition homotopy to two concatenated paths also identifies their composed equivalence with the one assigned to the concatenation.

source.place: Transport-of-units elaboration of Definitions 5.1.8 and 5.3.3; path-space definition of the homotopy fiber

proof.text: For $G_\bullet=\iota_\bullet B$, effectivity of groupoid objects in spaces gives $G_1\simeq G_0\times_{|G_\bullet|}G_0$ and surjectivity of $G_0\to|G_\bullet|$ on components. Consequently two points $b,b'$ of $X_B\simeq G_0$ have the same component in $\iota B$ exactly when the homotopy fiber $(G_1)_{b,b'}$ is nonempty, which by step 6 means an object equivalence between them. The same surjectivity for $\iota_\bullet A$ says that every component of $\iota A$ is represented by an object $a$. Thus surjectivity of $\pi_0\iota F$ says precisely that every $b$ is equivalent to some $F(a)$: in one direction choose an object representative $a$ for a preimage component, and in the other use the equivalence to identify the component of $b$ with that of $F(a)$. This includes empty object spaces.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 5.3.4; effectiveness of the groupoid object established in step 6

proof.text: For a strong monoidal functor $H^\otimes:\mathcal V^\otimes\to\mathcal W^\otimes$, postcomposition takes inert-preserving algebras and their coherent transformations to such algebras and transformations, and does not change object spaces. The equality $H^\otimes\circ(B\circ\Delta_f^{\mathrm{op}})=(H^\otimes\circ B)\circ\Delta_f^{\mathrm{op}}$ proves compatibility with restriction, including higher coherences. Its mapping-object formula is $(H_*A)(a,a')=H(A(a,a'))$. A fully faithful arrow stays fully faithful because $H$ takes an equivalence and its inverse homotopies to an equivalence. If $b$ is equivalent to $F(a)$ via $E^1_{\mathcal V}\to B$, strong monoidality identifies $H_*E^1_{\mathcal V}$ with $E^1_{\mathcal W}$; postcomposition gives the required equivalence in $H_*B$. Step 8 therefore proves preservation of essential surjectivity. By step 5 it also preserves Cartesian arrows, so this is a functor of the stated Cartesian fibrations.

source.place: Definition 3.6.12, Lemma 4.3.9 and Lemma 5.7.5, specialized to strong monoidal functors
